### 4.2.1 – What Is Slope?

* The **slope** of a line tells how steep it is — how fast y changes as x changes.
* It’s the **rate of change** between x and y.
* You can think of slope as the line’s *tilt* or *climb*.

:::{.real-world title="Slope as a Rate"}
If you earn $15 per hour, that’s a slope of 15 on a graph of pay vs. hours — your pay increases $15 for each additional hour you work.
:::

:::{.remember title="Formula for Slope"}
Between two points ((x_1, y_1)) and ((x_2, y_2)):
[
m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}
]
where (m) represents the slope.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Find the slope between (1, 2) and (4, 8)."}
:::

---

### 4.2.2 – Finding Slope From a Graph

* To find slope from a graph, pick two clear points on the line.
* Count the **rise** (change in y) and the **run** (change in x).
* Then use (m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}).

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_2/rise_run_example.png){width="300px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.think title="Reading Direction"}
Always read slope **left to right**, like you read a sentence.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Count the slope"}
Find the rise and run between two points on your graph, then compute (m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}).
:::

---

### 4.2.3 – Types of Slope

| Type          | Description               | Example  |
| ------------- | ------------------------- | -------- |
| **Positive**  | Line rises left to right  | (m > 0)  |
| **Negative**  | Line falls left to right  | (m < 0)  |
| **Zero**      | Line is flat (horizontal) | (y = 3)  |
| **Undefined** | Line is vertical (no run) | (x = -2) |

:::{.real-world title="What They Mean"}

* **Positive slope:** going uphill, savings increasing, temperature rising.
* **Negative slope:** going downhill, spending money, cooling down.
* **Zero slope:** no change — a flat road or steady balance.
* **Undefined slope:** vertical line — you’d have to “divide by zero,” which doesn’t make sense.
  :::

:::{.you-try-m title="Sketch examples"}
Draw one example of each type of slope on graph paper. Label each line with its slope.
:::

:::{.think title="When Two Lines Meet"}
If two lines have different slopes, they’ll **cross at one point**.  
That point has the same (x, y) values in both equations — it makes **both** true.
:::

---

### 4.2.4 – Slope in the Real World

:::{.real-world title="Comparing Slopes in Context"}

* A **wheelchair ramp** that rises 1 foot for every 12 feet forward has a slope of ( \frac{1}{12} ).
* A **hill** that rises 10 feet for every 20 feet forward has a slope of ( \frac{10}{20} = \frac{1}{2} ).
  Which one is steeper?
  :::

:::{.real-world title="Rates as Slopes"}

* A car traveling 60 miles per hour and a cyclist traveling 15 miles per hour both form straight lines on a distance-time graph.
* The car’s line is steeper because its **slope (rate of change)** is greater.
  :::

:::{.think title="What Slope Tells Us"}
The larger the slope, the faster the change.
The smaller the slope, the slower or flatter the change.
:::

---

:::{.remember title="Key Idea"}
Slope measures how y changes compared to x.
A **constant slope** means the line rises or falls evenly — that’s what makes it *linear*.
:::
